analysis.one_liner: Uses federal grants to wipe out medical debt and stops it from hitting credit reports.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up a federal grant program paying hospitals to cancel the medical debt their patients owe, and later expand to other providers. It would also ban collectors from pursuing any medical debt that existed before the law passed, block medical debt from appearing on credit reports, cap what nonprofit hospitals can charge uninsured patients, and outlaw interest on past-due medical bills. It was introduced in May 2024, sent to two House committees, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of Americans who carry medical debt would have it erased, and their credit reports would no longer show it, making it easier to rent, buy a car, or get a mortgage. Future patients would get clearer bills, notice of charity care, and no interest charges.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a competitive grant program in which the federal government pays hospitals to eliminate all eligible medical debt owed to them, prioritizing safety-net hospitals and debt from emergency care owed by low-income patients [S2].
Bars any debt collector or creditor from collecting medical debt incurred before enactment, and gives consumers a private right to sue for damages and attorney's fees if collectors try [S2].
Removes medical debt from credit reports within 30 days of enactment and requires credit bureaus to notify consumers of the removal [S2].
Caps what tax-exempt nonprofit hospitals can collect from uninsured patients at their generally billed amounts and prohibits charging interest on past-due medical bills [S2].

Requires providers to screen patients for charity care before bills come due and to send plain-language collection notices with language-assistance information in 15 languages, and forbids them from hiring collection agencies that ignore these rules [S2].
Directs the Health and Human Services Secretary to instruct federal health care programs to stop medical debt collections and to publish a public list of financial-assistance programs [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the buyout of hospital debt, and the bill text includes no dedicated funding or price tag. Hospitals and collection agencies would give up the medical debts they might have collected, and credit bureaus would lose medical debt as reportable information.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no funding source or appropriation for the grant program, so the multi-billion-dollar cost of buying out hospital debt would land on federal taxpayers or require separate legislation [S2].

Hospitals and collection agencies would absorb the loss of revenue from canceled debt, and providers could respond by tightening payment terms, requiring payment up front, or scaling back charity-care programs to protect their finances — a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.
Barring all medical debt reporting means lenders lose information some argue is relevant to creditworthiness, potentially tightening credit access in other ways.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households carrying medical debt, the benefits are direct and large: debt erased, credit reports cleaned, interest banned. The real drawback is cost — canceling existing debt nationwide is expensive and the bill leaves the financing open. The forward-looking billing and collection rules are modest and hard to argue against. The trade-off is mostly a question of public spending versus private debt relief, but Congress never engaged with it because the bill never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees the day it was introduced, then forwarded to a Health Subcommittee a week later, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Ro Khanna introduced the bill on May 8, 2024, with 12 Democratic cosponsors including Pramila Jayapal, Rashida Tlaib, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's wing allies such as Greg Casar and Summer Lee [S1][S2][S3].

The House referred it to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Financial Services Committee, a dual referral that means two committees would each have had to act before the bill could reach the floor [S1][S4].
On May 17, 2024, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded for the remainder of the Congress [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died without any committee or floor action [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and debt collectors keep the ability to pursue existing medical debt, and credit bureaus keep reporting it. No patient's medical debt was canceled by this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals and debt collectors keep collecting

industries.industry: Debt collection agencies and medical billing collectors
industries.note: The bill would ban collecting any pre-enactment medical debt and bar hospitals from hiring collectors that violate the new billing rules. Collectors' interest in keeping medical debt enforceable runs directly against patients' interest in erasing it.
The bill strips medical debt from consumer credit reports. Reporting bureaus lose a category of information and the collection ecosystem that feeds it.

industries.industry: Hospitals, especially nonprofit and safety-net hospitals
industries.note: Hospitals would receive federal grants to cancel debts they might never have collected in full — a financial upside — but would lose the ability to charge interest, collect above their generally billed amounts from uninsured patients, and use noncompliant collectors. The grant money would also entrench hospitals as the paid channel for debt relief rather than requiring them to forgive it as a condition of their tax exemption.
